What is the essential teaching in 'Responding with Skillful Karma'?

In 'Responding with Skillful Karma', the teaching opens with this observation: *"February 16, 2026, evening
Last night we talked about past karma, and in particular the skills you need to develop in constructing the present moment so that you don’t have to suffer from the results of past karma."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

Can you explain the teaching in the section 'Responding with Skillful Karma'?

This section teaches: *"Last night we talked about past karma, and in particular the skills you need to develop in constructing the present moment so that you don’t have to suffer from the results of past karma. Tonight I’d like to talk about the skills you need to develop so that you don’t respond unskillfully to the results either of past bad karma or of past good karma..."* The core instruction is to turn investigation inward (*opanayiko*) toward what is already present in body, speech, and mind — not to seek the Dhamma outside or in future states. Whatever theme this section addresses, the method is the same: sustained, patient, non-grasping awareness that allows the truth to reveal itself. As Ajahn Mun taught: when the mind sees clearly, there is no longer any need to go looking.

In this text, sati appears in this context: *"There’s an analogy that I’ve found useful—and, of course, this didn’t come from the Buddha—and that’s to make sure that your mind is not like a vacuum cleaner."* Understanding mindfulness (sati) — clear, present-moment awareness is not merely conceptual — it is meant to be verified directly. The Dhamma is *ehipassiko*: 'come and see for yourself.' Bring the quality described by sati into direct investigation: where is it present in your current experience? When seen clearly, each of these Pāli terms dissolves from abstract concept into living reality.
